title: Nehemiah's wall (Nehemiah 2–4)
hook: a cupbearer weeps, prays, and rebuilds with a trowel in one hand and a sword in the other
carry: let us rise up and build

segments.voice: Yesterday, foundation day under Cyrus, when the old wept and the young shouted. Your line was joy and grief, one sound. Where did you hear both at once? Day seven hundred forty-two.

Nehemiah has a good job. He's cupbearer to the king of Persia, the man who hands the king his wine. Then visitors arrive from Judah, and he asks how Jerusalem is doing. Badly, they say. The wall is broken down and the gates are burned. Nehemiah writes: "I sat down and wept, and mourned certain days, and fasted, and prayed before the God of heaven." Later he's serving wine, and the king notices his face. Why is your face sad, when you're not sick? Nehemiah is frightened. He's about to ask the king for something enormous. And between the king's question and his answer, there's one half-line that's today.

The king asks, what do you want? And Nehemiah writes: "So I prayed to the God of heaven." That's it. No time for a long prayer. A breath of a prayer between a question and an answer, standing beside the throne with the wine. Then he asks: send me to rebuild the city. And the king says yes. In Jerusalem, Nehemiah doesn't start with a speech. He goes out at night, quietly, with a few men, and rides around the ruins to see the damage for himself. Only then does he gather the people and tell them what he saw and how God had helped him. Their answer: "Let us rise up and build. So they strengthened their hands for this good work." Chapter three is a long list of names and gates: who repaired which stretch, families, priests, goldsmiths, apothecaries, some working on the section by their own house. Then the mocking starts. Sanballat and Tobiah, local officials who oppose the work, laugh at it. Tobiah's joke is in the text: "even that which they build, if a fox go up, he shall even break down their stone wall." Then the mocking turns into threats of attack. So Nehemiah sets guards, and the builders change how they work. "Every one with one of his hands wrought in the work, and with the other hand held a weapon." A trowel in one hand, a sword at the side. They kept building anyway. Some Christians read this as a picture of steady work under pressure: you pray in a breath, you look at the damage honestly, you build your own stretch, and you don't stop because someone is laughing.
screen: `ONE HAND WORKS, ONE HOLDS A WEAPON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk around one broken wall. Settle, and breathe. Like Nehemiah riding out at night, look honestly at one thing in your life that's broken: a friendship, a habit, a room, a promise you didn't keep. Don't fix it yet. Just see the damage clearly, without blaming anyone. Then find one stretch, the small section by your own house, that you could repair. If you pray, you can do what Nehemiah did between two sentences and pray to the God of heaven. If you don't, just name the stretch. The bell holds the time.
Nehemiah's wall. Jerusalem's broken wall, rebuilt by builders each working their own stretch, with one hand on the work and the other on a weapon.

Your line: let us rise up and build. This week went from a muddy river to an opened eye, a lost book, an exile, a queen's courage, and a foundation. Today, repair one broken thing, even a small one. Day seven hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Christians sometimes read Nehemiah when a church or community starts a building or repair project, and some take up his quick prayer between two sentences as a model for praying in the middle of a hard conversation.

pray to the God of heaven, then ask to go and rebuild.

original.note: Hebrew: let us rise up and build, the people's answer in Nehemiah 2:18.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about building a wall.
what it means: a cupbearer weeps, prays in a breath, sees the damage himself, and the people build their own stretches under mockery.
what a scholar hears: Nehemiah 3 is a long list of names and gates, and Nehemiah 4:17 has the builders working with one hand and holding a weapon with the other.
